title: Counterfactual
pitch: See your future before you choose it. Name a big decision, watch it branch into possible paths, protect what matters, and decide with an agent by your side.
about_excerpt: See your future before you choose it. Name a big decision, watch it branch into possible paths, protect what matters, and decide with an agent by your side. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Dynamic paths Home page Flight Recorder for tool calls Decisions, assumptions, and goals Testing with WebMCP tools Chrome extension Tutorial mode Inspiration AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of taking actions across the web, but users do not always get a clear picture of the consequences before those actions happen. A decision like buying a car can affect several competing goals at once, yet most financial tools reduce that complexity to a single static calculation. I built Counterfactual around a simple question: what if an agent could show you several possible futures before asking you to commit to one? Instead of immediately executing an action, Counterfactual gives the agent and user a shared space to explore alternatives, revise assumptions, understand tradeoffs, and decide together which future—if any—should become real. What it does Counterfactual is a WebMCP-powered decision simulator and permission layer for the agentic web. Through WebMCP, an AI agent can discover structured tools exposed by Counterfactual, read the user's financial assumptions, create alternative scenarios, simulate their outcomes, and compare them. Counterfactual turns those scenarios into explorable futures with dynamic visualizations that show how each decision affects the user's finances and protected goals. Users can change an assumption at any time and immediately see every future recalculate. A built-in WebMCP Flight Recorder makes the agent's behavior visible by recording each tool it discovers and invokes, along with its arguments, risk level, origin, status, and results. Rather than receiving only the agent's final recommendation, users can inspect the actual sequence of actions that produced it. Most importantly, Counterfactual distinguishes between exploring a future and making it real . Read-only and simulation tools can run freely, but when an agent attempts a consequential action, Counterfactual pauses execution and requires explicit human approval. The result is a simple principle: agents can explore autonomously, but humans retain control over commitment. How I built it I built Counterfactual with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and client-side state . Its scenario engine uses deterministic calculations so the agent's conclusions and the visual interface always operate from the same source of truth. Counterfactual exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . These include tools for reading financial state, defining a decision, protecting goals, creating scenarios, comparing outcomes, simulating purchases, and committing to a selected scenario. Each tool has a natural-language description, JSON Schema input definition, validation, and metadata describing its behavior and risk. To support browsers that do not yet implement WebMCP natively, Counterfactual uses the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill package. A thin compatibility layer detects the available context—native, polyfilled, legacy, or fallback—and registers the same tool surface against it. Every invocation, whether initiated manually or by an external agent, passes through the same execution and logging pipeline. Calls are timestamped and risk-tagged before appearing in the Flight Recorder. Consequential actions go through an additional policy and approval layer before they can modify committed state. The approval is tied to that specific proposed action, preventing an agent from silently turning a simulation into a real commitment. I also tested the WebMCP integration end-to-end using Google's webmcp-evals CLI. That testing uncovered an issue that was invisible through Counterfactual's own UI but appeared when a tool was invoked through the actual WebMCP path. Fixing it helped ensure the project works through the protocol itself rather than only through a scripted demo. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was building against an experimental standard whose API and browser support are still evolving. Counterfactual needed to target the current document.modelContext API while remaining usable in browsers and agents relying on earlier or unsupported implementations. Another challenge was maintaining a single source of truth across the agent, editable controls, scenario calculations, visual branches, and Flight Recorder. A tool call could not simply generate an answer—it had to operate on the same live state the user was seeing and immediately update the rest of the experience. The final challenge was designing meaningful human oversight without making the agent feel unnecessarily constrained. Requiring approval for every tool call would defeat much of the value of an agent, while allowing every action to execute automatically would remove meaningful user control. Counterfactual therefore treats risk as a gradient: agents can read, simulate, fork, and compare independently, while actions that create real commitments stop at the point where human judgment matters most. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that Counterfactual uses WebMCP as a core interaction model , rather than adding it as a superficial integration. The agent does not simply fill out a form or operate a scripted demo—it collaborates with the user inside a shared decision environment. I also built a complete flow from tool discovery → simulation → comparison → recommendation → approval . Users can see what the agent is doing, inspect how it reached its recommendation, modify the assumptions themselves, explore alternative futures, and ultimately reject or approve the proposed action. Most importantly, Counterfactual turns an abstract AI safety problem into something tangible: consequential agent actions become forkable futures that people can inspect before making them real. What I learned I learned that WebMCP is more than a reliable way for agents to interact with websites. It can enable entirely new forms of human-agent collaboration . Structured tools allow an agent and an interface to share the same capabilities and application state without relying on fragile DOM interpretation or browser automation. I also learned that confirmation alone is not enough to provide meaningful user control. Before approving an action, people need to understand what they are approving, which goals may be affected, what alternatives exist, and whether the action can be reversed. Building Counterfactual showed me how structured tool schemas, deterministic application logic, risk classification, and visual design can work together to make agent behavior more transparent, understandable, and trustworthy. Why my use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Many agent experiences focus on reading the web: searching, summarizing, and answering questions. Counterfactual focuses on the harder problem— what happens when an agent can act on something that matters? That is where WebMCP becomes especially valuable. Counterfactual's decision process maps naturally onto a set of well-defined tools such as get_financial_state , define_decision , set_protected_goal , fork_scenario , compare_scenarios , and commit_scenario . Those tools also span a genuine risk gradient. Reading financial state is fundamentally different from simulating a hypothetical decision, and both are fundamentally different from committing to one. Counterfactual uses that distinction to determine when an agent can proceed independently and when control must return to the user. Instead of bolting permissions onto a chat interface after the fact, the application's capabilities, schemas, risk levels, and guardrails are part of the same structured tool environment the agent discovers and uses. How it creates a better user experience Instead of interacting with a black box that eventually reports, "I looked into it and think you should wait," Counterfactual lets the user see what the agent actually explored. Each hypothetical future becomes a visible branch with its own projected balance, goal impact, and explanation. The Flight Recorder shows the sequence of tool calls that produced those futures, including their arguments, risk levels, and results. That makes questions like "Why did the agent recommend this?" answerable by inspecting what actually happened rather than trusting a secondhand explanation. Counterfactual also includes a Manual Tool Console that lets users invoke the same tools themselves through the same schemas and Flight Recorder pipeline. The human and the agent are therefore operating the same system rather than two separate interfaces. And when an action would turn a hypothetical future into a real commitment, execution stops. Counterfactual shows the consequences and requires explicit approval before anything changes. The user sees the future before they inherit its consequences.
